source: Norenzayan, Smith, Kim, Nisbett (2002) Cultural preferences for formal versus intuitive reasoning, Study 1 (rule learning)
finding: All groups learned categories equally well by exemplar memory. When a rule conflicted with similarity to a past exemplar, East Asians made more extra errors than European Americans.
numbers: Rule group: culture x item type F(2,67)=3.81 p<.05; negative-positive error gap larger for East Asians than European Americans F(1,67)=4.97 p<.05. Exemplar-memory control: no culture effect F(2,77)=1.18 ns. Three groups: European American, Asian American, East Asian (Chinese, Korean) students at a US university.
limits: Small cells. Tested in English at a US university. Interaction is modest (p<.05).
agent_relevance: A rule versus similarity conflict is where style differences appear, not in raw ability. A scaffold should make the rule-versus-resemblance choice explicit.

source: Norenzayan et al. (2002) Study 2 (classify vs judge similarity)
finding: Task wording mattered. Asked which group the target belongs to, all cultures picked the rule. Asked which group it is more similar to, East Asians flipped to family resemblance and European Americans did not.
numbers: Belong-to condition: rule 67% vs resemblance 33%, F(1,100)=44.40 p<.001, no culture x response interaction F(2,100)=1.25. Similar-to condition: culture x response F(2,51)=8.01 p<.005; European Americans rule 69% vs 31%, East Asians rule 41% vs 59% (t(17)=2.09 p=.05), Asian Americans 46% vs 54%. n=18 per cell in similar-to.
limits: Only 18 per group in the key condition; East Asian effect is borderline (p=.05). The culture difference was seen only under similarity instructions.
agent_relevance: Instruction wording ('belongs to' vs 'similar to') moves categorisation more than culture does. For an LLM, prompt wording is the lever: ask for rule-based or similarity-based grouping explicitly.

source: Norenzayan et al. (2002) Studies 3 and 4 (typicality and belief bias)
finding: Koreans were more swayed by typicality of premise categories in arguments (Study 3). In Study 4 Koreans erred more on concrete syllogisms with believable conclusions.
numbers: Study 3: typicality effect culture x argument type F(2,253)=4.67 p<.01; Koreans stronger than European Americans F(1,253)=9.09 p<.005. Study 4: Koreans less likely to say 'yes' (response bias F(1,184)=14.41 p<.001); abstract-argument accuracy 45.1% vs 48.5%, t<1.
limits: Study 4 later challenged on response-bias grounds (see b04).
agent_relevance: Typicality pulls judgment toward similarity; a reasoning agent needs a check that separates logical form from believable content.

source: Unsworth & Medin (2005) Cultural differences in belief bias associated with deductive reasoning? Cognitive Science 29, 525-529
finding: Re-analysis of Norenzayan et al. Experiment 4. Koreans were simply more conservative in saying 'valid'. Once hit and correct-rejection rates were averaged, European Americans were no better than Koreans at judging validity of concrete arguments.
numbers: Reanalysis of three conditions (abstract, concrete-believable, concrete-nonbelievable); no accuracy advantage for European Americans once response bias is handled.
quote: may be misleading because response bias needs to be addressed
limits: Comment on one experiment; does not touch the categorisation studies (1, 2).
agent_relevance: A failed-interpretation case: separate bias (threshold) from sensitivity (accuracy) when comparing styles or models.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2, replication of Norenzayan et al. 2002 Study 2 (aggregate)
finding: The instruction effect replicated strongly worldwide: 'belongs to' gave more rule-based answers than 'similar to'. This was the pre-registered test. The between-culture contrast was not the replicated target.
numbers: N=7,396. Belong-to: rule 64% (SD 25); similar-to: rule 44% (SD 21). t(7,227.6)=37.05, d=0.86, 95% CI [0.81,0.91]. Original: European Americans d=0.00 and East Asians d=0.67 for the condition effect.
limits: The pre-registered contrast was across instructions, not across cultures. Original cultural claim was only tested within the similar-to condition.
agent_relevance: Task framing is robust and large (d=0.86). Good evidence that prompt framing changes category strategy.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2, WEIRDness moderation of the Norenzayan effect
finding: The Norenzayan effect was one of only three of 28 ML2 effects significantly moderated by sample WEIRDness. But the cultural difference ran opposite to the original claim.
numbers: 3 of 28 effects moderated (Huang 2014, Knobe 2003, Norenzayan 2002). Median Cohen's d in WEIRD samples: originals 0.60, replications 0.15. Aggregate effect for Norenzayan d=0.86.
limits: Original had no stated theory about cultural differences in the condition effect, so the inverse pattern is not a clean refutation. WEIRDness is a country-level score, not East Asian status.
agent_relevance: Cultural moderation of categorisation framing is not reliable; the framing effect itself is.

source: Schimmelpfennig et al. (2024) reanalysis of Many Labs 2 cultural variability (Communications Psychology)
finding: Reanalysis finds little cultural variability and low power to detect cultural heterogeneity in ML2. Other ways of measuring culture slightly raised effect sizes but changed no conclusion.
numbers: Seen only in a search summary; no figures read.
limits: Not opened; description from a search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Warns that a null cultural moderation may reflect low power, not absence.

source: Klein, Lin, Radford, Masuda, Choi, Lien, Yeh, Boff (2009) Cultural differences in cognition: Rosetta Phase I, categorisation task (Psychological Reports 105, 659-674)
finding: Six analytic-holistic measures in Japan, Korea, Taiwan and the USA. Exclusion and categorisation differences were reported, but categorisation held only in response time, not in choices.
numbers: N=379, age 17-24, 64.6% women. Similar condition n=45/44/50/46 (Japan/Korea/Taiwan/USA). Holistic-response count did not differ, F(3,181)=2.01 ns; US slower, t(89)=4.71 p<.001 vs Japan. Rule condition: no differences, matching Norenzayan 2002.
limits: Student samples; the authors say two tasks were 'confounded by unrelated group differences'. Exploratory.
agent_relevance: A partial replication: the similarity route is slower for Americans, not different in choice. Do not assume a strong choice difference.

source: Klein et al. (2009) Rosetta Phase I, Framed Line Test
finding: On the framed line test the East Asian groups did better than Americans in both relative and absolute conditions. The original (Kitayama 2003) expected the absolute condition to favour Americans. That part did not replicate.
numbers: Relative-judgment errors F(3,375)=16.92 p<.001; absolute-judgment errors F(3,375)=18.26 p<.001; all three East Asian groups better than USA in both.
limits: Authors say group differences in other abilities confounded the comparison.
agent_relevance: Focal versus context attention results can reflect general task skill; use a control condition before reading style into a score.

source: Lacko et al. (2025) Investigating the geography of thought across 11 countries, J Exp Psychol Gen 154(2), 325-346
finding: Large preregistered study with Navon and embedded-figures tasks found cross-cultural differences, but not along the predicted East-West line.
numbers: N=993 students, 11 countries (Armenia, Australia, Brazil, Bulgaria, Czechia, Germany, Ghana, Philippines, Slovakia, Taiwan, Turkiye). Reaction-time modeling. Individualism and long-term orientation related to both styles.
limits: Not opened (paywalled; details from search snippets). Uses simple perceptual tasks, not categorisation.
agent_relevance: The strongest recent null for a global East-West style dimension; treat the 'two styles' idea as weak.

source: Cross-cultural analysis of eye-movement patterns in visual scene perception, seven cultural samples (Scientific Reports 2025)
finding: Eye tracking on scenes in seven samples. Everyone looked longer at focal objects than at the background. Culture differed, but the ranking did not follow East versus West.
numbers: About 408 participants (F(6,401)=12.77, omega squared=0.15). Dwell on focal object: Ghana 1895 ms (longest), Taiwan 1528 ms (shortest), Germany 1533 ms (nearly tied with Taiwan). Focal-minus-background gap: Ghana g=1.95; Taiwan g=0.44; others 1.3 to 2.1. Saccade length F(6,163.2)=7.43, omega squared=0.18; 7.06 deg Ghana to 8.31 deg Taiwan.
limits: Taiwan shows the weakest object bias (as expected), but Germany looks as 'holistic' as Taiwan on dwell. Two Turkish samples were not equivalent.
agent_relevance: Attention measures vary by culture but not along a clean analytic-holistic axis.

source: Carlson et al. (2025) Cultural differences in visual attention emerge in infancy (Infancy)
finding: 15-month-old Japanese infants looked at backgrounds longer than US infants, with the gap largest for objects with eyes. Japanese parents also mentioned the background more.
numbers: Japan n=45, US n=52 infants; analysed n=84 (faces), 80 (caterpillar), 82 (book). Background looking about twice as long in cartoons.
limits: Small samples; parent talk did not correlate with infant behaviour on the earlier tasks, so socialization is not shown.
agent_relevance: Context sensitivity may be early and perceptual, so not purely trained by instruction.

source: Carstensen, Kim, Choi, Walker (2026) Relational reasoning across cultures: Korea, US, China (Behavioral Sciences 16, 1406)
finding: Relational versus object bias in a match-to-sample task. Korean children fall between US (object bias) and China (relational bias), closer to US. Adults show no bias.
numbers: Korean 18-30 month-olds n=91: same condition 28/41 correct (68%, BF10=4.07); different condition 25/50 at chance. Korean 3-year-olds n=55: 29 chose relational (53%, BF10=0.34). Korean adults n=60: 52% relational (BF10=0.31). 4-year-olds KR 79%/85% and US 77%/80%, above chance.
limits: Bayesian stopping rule, small groups. No clear bias in Korea; the East-West pair is not simple.
agent_relevance: Relational bias is a continuum and fades in adults; no fixed 'relational style'.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought, Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: The founding review. Claims East Asians are holistic (field, relations, dialectic) and Westerners analytic (objects, categories, rules). Reports attention, categorisation and covariation studies.
numbers: Masuda and Nisbett fish scenes: Japanese made about 70% more background statements and about 100% more relational statements; equal focal-fish mentions. Chiu 1972 triads and Ji and Nisbett adult Chinese vs American relation-versus-category grouping.
limits: Narrative review; many cited studies were unpublished or small. The social-origin account is speculation.
agent_relevance: Source of the framing our schema should treat as a hypothesis, not a fact about minds.

source: Nisbett & Norenzayan (2002) Culture and cognition, Stevens' Handbook: Choi, Nisbett, Smith (1997) induction
finding: Koreans used category coverage less than Americans in induction, unless the category was made salient by naming it in the conclusion. That cue moved Koreans and not Americans.
numbers: Described qualitatively in the chapter; no figures taken.
limits: Secondary summary read; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Salient cues can switch categorisation use; a cheap prompt-side lever.

source: Hedden, Park, Nisbett, Ji et al. (2000) background binding of words, as summarised in the 2001 review
finding: Chinese, not Americans, recalled words better when printed on social backgrounds, suggesting the background served as a retrieval cue.
numbers: Qualitative description only.
limits: Secondary summary.
agent_relevance: Context-bound memory can help retrieval but also contaminate; a scaffold can control context.

source: Ji, Peng, Nisbett (2000) covariation detection, as summarised in the 2001 review
finding: Chinese participants reported more covariation than Americans on arbitrary figure pairs and were better calibrated; Americans showed strong primacy.
numbers: Actual covariation ran 0.00 to 0.60; no sample counts in the review.
limits: Secondary; sample sizes not seen.
agent_relevance: Calibration and primacy are measurable; ties to guarding against anchoring on first evidence.

source: Sun & Wang (2025) The fragility of 'cultural tendencies' in LLMs
finding: Replication of Lu, Song, Zhang with 8 LLMs and 30-60 items per task. Prompt language had minimal effect. Effects appeared only in a few models on single tasks.
numbers: gpt-4.1, gemini-2.5, claude-sonnet-4, grok-4, kimi-k2, deepseek-V3, ernie-4.5, qwen3-30b; temperature 0. Overall language effect p=0.15 (framing), 0.25 (attribution), 1.0 (syllogism), 0.917 (interpersonal). Model origin: no effect.
limits: Original test items were not released, so not an exact replication; not a categorisation task.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on prompting in Chinese or English to switch thinking style.

source: Hu et al. (2026) Machine Culture, 2x2 model origin x prompt language, 8 tasks incl. triad categorisation
finding: Triad (relational vs categorical) task contradicted human expectations: the US model paired more relationally than the Chinese model. Prompt language made no difference.
numbers: Task 4 R-C score: US model 8.10 (SD 1.44) vs Chinese model 6.04 (SD 1.54); Chinese vs English prompts 7.10 vs 7.04, n.s. GPT-4o vs ERNIE 4.5; temperature 1; 400 observations per task.
limits: Two model families only; model-judged scoring for some tasks.
agent_relevance: The LLM's categorisation style is a property of the model and prompt wording, not a switchable culture.

source: Hu et al. (2026) Machine Culture: Cultural Reversal and Service Persona Camouflage
finding: English prompts gave higher contextual attention than Chinese ones. RLHF-tuned models collapsed variance in affective tasks to a helpful-assistant persona.
numbers: Same design; attribution task: Chinese model higher on both collective (3.17 vs 2.81) and individual (4.75 vs 4.67) attribution.
limits: Interpretation is the authors' account.
agent_relevance: Alignment training can wash out style variance; style tests on aligned models may measure persona.

source: Jin et al. (2023) The cultural psychology of LLMs: is ChatGPT a holistic or analytic thinker?
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 scored holistic on the Analysis-Holism Scale and a 20-item triad categorisation test. Robust across temperature and prompt changes.
numbers: N=10 runs per cell. AHS GPT-3.5 5.35 (SD 0.11), GPT-4 5.01 vs human norm 4.87 (N=702, SD 0.49). TCT GPT-3.5 0.87, GPT-4 0.85 relational share. GPT-3.5 SCS-Independent 6.98 vs norm 4.73.
limits: Runs are the unit of N so p-values are inflated; self-report scales given to an LLM; no human norm for the triad task (compared with Chinese provincial data).
agent_relevance: LLMs prefer relational grouping on triads, contrary to the guess that Western training data means analytic.

source: Lu, Song, Zhang (2025) Cultural tendencies in generative AI, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Reported that GPT and ERNIE respond more holistically and interdependently in Chinese than in English, and that a Chinese-persona prompt shifts English answers.
numbers: Per Sun and Wang: 4-12 items per task, 7 tasks, 2 models. No other numbers seen.
limits: Not opened (publisher page unavailable); described via the critique and a search summary. Items were withheld.
agent_relevance: Prompt-language style switching is contested (see b18, b19).

source: Methods caveat across LLM studies: run-level N, item count, temperature
finding: Jin et al. fixed temperature and prompts and tested robustness; Hu et al. used temperature 1 with 400 observations; Sun and Wang used temperature 0, which removes variance.
numbers: Jin: N=10 per cell. Hu: 400 per task. Sun and Wang: temperature 0, 30-60 items.
limits: Different designs give different power; results are not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Report item count, number of runs and temperature for any categorisation test of our own agent.

source: Cross-study synthesis: what held up for categorisation and attention (this agent's reading)
finding: Held up: instruction-driven shift between rule and resemblance (d=0.86). Mixed: culture gap in resemblance use (n=18 per group originally; inverse in ML2 moderation). Not held: a clean East-West axis in simple perceptual tasks (N=993, 11 countries) and LLM prompt-language switching.
numbers: Numbers from b05, b06, b10, b18, b19.
limits: Synthesis; relies on a partly unopened source (Lacko).
agent_relevance: For our agent, treat style as a state set by the prompt, not a trait.

source: Norenzayan et al. (2002) Study 1 control: exemplar memory equal across cultures
finding: Ability control: no culture differences when no rule was available. Learning improved across four trials equally in all groups.
numbers: Errors fell from 20.7% to 11.3% (F(3,201)=6.43 p<.001); no culture main effect F(2,67)=1.79 ns; RT fell from 5586 ms to 3294 ms.
limits: Same small samples.
agent_relevance: Rules out ability as the source; the difference is strategy choice under conflict.
